title: Great Lakes Sturgeon May Live 400+ Years, Study Suggests
summary: In the early 1600s, a telescope first spotted Jupiter's moons, horse riding was the fastest land travel, and smallpox was rampant. Four hundred years later, some fish in the Great Lakes may have been alive the entire time. Research published this year in the Journal of Fish Biology suggests lake sturgeon (Acipenser fulvescens) can live far longer than scientists thought. The study concludes males may reach 435 years — nearly three times the age of the previous record-holder, a 154-year-old sturgeon caught in 1953. "All sturgeon species now need to be reassessed for their age because of this paper," says ichthyologist Prosanta Chakrabarty of Louisiana State University, who wasn't involved in the work. Lake sturgeon are cartilaginous fish whose ancestors swam with dinosaurs 200 million years ago. Today they're the largest fish in the Great Lakes, typically four to six feet long and 30 to 80 pounds. Their average lifespan was thought to be 50 to 100 years. The problem: aging a wild fish is hard. Each dark ring on a sturgeon's fin spine marks a year, but in old, slow-growing fish the rings crowd together and become impossible to count. So Edward Baker of the Michigan Department of Natural Resources and colleagues used a different method. From 1980 to 2024, they caught thousands of sturgeon across five Upper Great Lakes waterways, measured them, and injected transponder tags — the same kind vets use for pets. When a tagged fish was recaptured, sometimes 42 years later, they could measure its growth. From that data, they estimated ages: some males up to 435 years, females up to 292. The team suggests winter torpor — a low-energy state — may help sturgeon live so long. Chakrabarty calls the method "a little more quaint than radiocarbon dating," and says he'd only call these the oldest vertebrates after more testing.
why_it_matters: If lake sturgeon really live several times longer than assumed, then the rules used to protect them — fishing limits, recovery targets and monitoring periods — may be far too short for a species that matures slowly and breeds rarely, which is a problem shared by many long-lived animals in a changing climate.

background_read: The Great Lakes are five enormous lakes along the border between the United States and Canada, and together they hold roughly a fifth of the world's surface fresh water. Lake sturgeon were once extremely abundant there, but heavy fishing in the 1800s for meat and caviar crashed their numbers, and because the fish mature slowly and spawn only every few years, populations have recovered very slowly.

Prosanta Chakrabarty, quoted in the article, is an ichthyologist — a scientist who studies fish — at Louisiana State University, and the Michigan Department of Natural Resources is the state agency that manages fish and wildlife in Michigan and helped run the tagging work. The Journal of Fish Biology is a scientific journal that publishes fish research.

Judging the age of a long-lived wild animal has always been difficult, and scientists have borrowed a technique from archaeology: radiocarbon dating, which measures a radioactive form of carbon that builds up in tissues. Greenland sharks, for example, have been aged this way using proteins in their eyes and are often described as the longest-living vertebrates, with lifespans estimated in the centuries.

If a commercially and culturally important fish lives several times longer than assumed, that changes conservation maths. A species that may take a century to mature and breeds rarely can look healthy while quietly disappearing, because managers may set protection periods far shorter than one generation.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — a breakthrough for fish biology and conservation
perspectives.description: Supporters argue the 42-year tagging record is unusually strong evidence, and that a much longer lifespan would explain why sturgeon populations recover so slowly. If the species needs centuries, not decades, to replace itself, conservation plans can be redesigned around that reality.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — the method is indirect and the claim may be premature
perspectives.description: Chakrabarty himself calls the technique 'a little more quaint than radiocarbon dating' and says he would only call these the oldest vertebrates after more testing. Age estimates built from growth rates of recaptured fish depend on assumptions, and a handful of very old individuals can inflate the numbers.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — a familiar problem in ageing wild animals
perspectives.description: Estimating the lifespan of long-lived species has always been hard: fin-spine rings crowd together, teeth wear out and tagged individuals must be caught twice. Radiocarbon dating, including the carbon left by mid-20th-century nuclear tests, became a standard cross-check for whales and sharks, and tagging studies are an older but still useful approach.

The article's headline claim is that all sturgeon species now need their ages re-examined, which could trigger a wave of new studies, more collaboration between agencies and universities, and a rethink of how old age itself works in cold-blooded animals.
